To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the prevalence of hypertension was high in the Caribbean unemployed population, but was controlled in only 17% of men and in 37% of women receiving anti-hypertensive treatment; (2) the prevalence was higher than in an employed Caribbean population and lower than in an employed metropolitan French one, suggesting the importance of access to health care for the control of hypertension; (3) the high prevalence of obesity in the Caribbean populations suggests the importance of primary prevention.
in a Caribbean population, hypertension was highly prevalent, poorly controlled and associated with obesity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the burden of hypertension in the Caribbean.
the burden of hypertension, which relates to the development and control of hypertension.
the development and control of hypertension in three populations: two Caribbean (unemployed and employed) and one metropolitan French (employed).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the prevalence of hypertension is high in the Caribbean and that the access to health care does not seem to be the main factor of this prevalence, whereas it seems to have an impact on the control of hypertension.
the burden of hypertension is high in the Caribbean population studied and that it is mainly related to the high prevalence of hypertension and not to the low level of blood pressure control.
the burden of hypertension is higher in the Caribbean, and in the unemployed population, than in metropolitan France.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the context of good access to health services, a large proportion of the burden of hypertension can be attributed to poor control of hypertension, while a large proportion of patients remain unidentified.
the burden of hypertension is higher in the unemployed Caribbean population compared to the employed French population.
the burden of arterial hypertensions in a population relates both to primary prevention (development of hypertension), and secondary prevention (control of hypertension).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of hypertension and obesity is high in an unemployed population with good access to health services in the Caribbean, and that primary prevention should be reinforced.
the burden of arterial hypertention is high in the Caribbean and is related to both the development of the disease and its control.
the burden of hypertension in a given population relates to the level of development of the disease (primary prevention) as well as to the level of control of the disease (secondary prevention).
